newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore to raise water cost four-fold by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Singapore to raise water cost four-fold by 2000.

text.p: Singapore will raise the price of water four-fold by 2000 to spur conservation, Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said on Tuesday.
He told a news conference the radical rise was to drive home the fact that water is a strategic resource in a small country largely dependent on Malaysia for supplies.
Lee said the government aimed eventually to make the total price of water least Singapore $2 per cubic metre. Some users now pay as little as 56 cents per cubic metre.
Lee said a recent diplomatic row with Malaysia was not a reason for the price increase.
"It is not a serious issue with the Malaysian government," Lee said, referring to recent calls by some low-level Malaysian politicians during the row for a review of water supplies to Singapore.
He said the Malaysian government had already guaranteed there would be no water supply problems.
Lee said that whether or not Singapore's water supplies were threatened, it would face a shortage by 2011, when the first of two water agreements with Malaysia expires.

The second expires in 2061. Singapore can draw up to 250 million gallons per day. It consumes about 240 million gallons. The calls for a review of the water deals came after Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew was deemed to have insulted Malaysia in March.

Lee called Malaysia's southern state of Johore "notorious for shootings, muggings and carjackings," sparking a furious exchange, which died at government level when Lee persuaded a court to withdraw an affidavit in which he made the remark.
Last week Singapore members of parliament urged the government to find an alternative to Malaysian water.
The rise in water costs now, including wastewater treatment fees, means monthly bills will rise by about 120 percent for households, and 30 percent for businesses by 2000.
The first rate hike will occur in July and the price increase will also reflect a water conservation tax.
Lee said pricing was an important and effective mechanism to get consumers to conserve water.
A government statement said it was policy not only to recover the full costs of supplying water but also to reflect the scarcity of it and the high incremental cost of additional water.
Lee said: "We have been watching all the various rate adjustments we are making...so that it doesn't cause a sudden shock to the consumer price index," Lee said.
